To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the hard gluonic contributions to the first moments of g1 are gauge invariant, and that these contributions are zero in dimensional regularization.
the first moment of spin‐dependent structure functions is gauge invariant and that there is no hard gluonic contribution in dimensional regularization.

the hard gluonic corrections to the first moment are zero in the standard dimensional regularization scheme, and nonzero in the dimensional regularization scheme with a regulator that does not allow shifts of loop momentum.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the question of whether or not the gauge invarience of Green’s functions can be used as an additional constraint on the regulator of the quark distributions in order to obtain the hard gluonic correction to the first moment.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
there is no hard gluonic contribution of the type discussed in the literature to the first moment, or indeed to any other moment, of g1.
there is no hard gluonic contribution of the first moment of proton’s structure function g1.

the first moment of a gauge invariant g1 is zero, while the first moment of an arbitrary g1 can be nonvanishing, but only at the price of introducing a gauge variant contribution to the first moments of quark distributions.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the hard gluonic contributions to the first moment vanish in a gauge invariant regularization scheme.
the hard gluonic contributions to the first moment are not well‐defined quantities.
there is a hard gluonic correction to the first moment, if one is willing to abandon gauge invariance, analyticity, or the operator‐product expansion.
The main takeaway from our work is that

, while it is not necessary to assume a vanishing hard gluonic correction to the first moment in order to reconcile the results of the lattice calculations with the experimental data, the hard gluonic correction is not gauge invariant, and, as such, it is not clear that it is physical.
the hard gluonic contributions to g1 and g2 are entirely determined by the gauge invariant, local, spin‐dependent quarks distributions.
the size of a hard gluonic correction to the first moment depends crucially on the convention used in separating the quark and gluon distributions.
